title: Estimating by decomposition
summary: Turn a quantity you cannot look up into a product of quantities you can estimate.
prereqText: You only need multiplication and powers of ten.

blocks.html: A colleague claims the city needs 2,000 new piano tuners. Before you can argue, you need a sense of how many pianos and tuners exist. No table lists these numbers, but you can reason towards them.

Think of the estimate as a chain of links. Each link is a quantity you can guess within a factor of a few. Multiply the links and the errors partly cancel, because some guesses are too high and others too low.
blocks.limits: Errors cancel only when they are independent. If every factor is biased the same way (for example, you assume the whole city is like your neighbourhood), they compound instead.

blocks.purpose: Show the estimate as a product of factors, each with its own range.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a row: number of people, pianos per person, tunings per piano per year, and division by the number of tunings one tuner does per year.

blocks.prompt: If you double the share of households with a piano, what happens to the estimate?

feedback.1: Every factor multiplies the result, so no factor is negligible.
feedback.2: Only factors that appear squared would quadruple it.

blocks.explanation: The estimate is a product of the factors, so it scales linearly with each one.

blocks.html:
Write the target as a formula of factors whose units cancel. For each factor, give a low and a high value you would be surprised to see exceeded. Use the geometric mean of the bounds as your point estimate. The order of magnitude of the result is usually right even when individual factors are off by a factor of two.

Why the geometric mean. If you think a factor lies between 1 and 100, the arithmetic mean (about 50) sits almost at the top of your range, so it treats 100 as far more likely than 1. The geometric mean, √(1 × 100) = 10, is the same number of times away from each bound. Fermi factors are uncertain by multiples, not by fixed amounts, so the middle that matters is the one measured in multiples.

Check the units before the numbers. Write each factor with its unit, such as people, households per person or tunings per piano per year, and cancel them on paper. If the result is not in the unit you asked for (here, tuners), a factor is missing or upside down. Most large Fermi errors are a missing or inverted factor, not a bad guess.

Find the factor that matters most. Once you have an estimate, ask which factor you are least sure of, and redo the product with its low and high bound. If the answer changes by a factor of ten, that factor is where to look for data first. If no plausible bound moves the answer near the claim you are testing, you can reject the claim without better data.

blocks.title: Piano tuners in a city of 1 million

steps.html: Pianos: about 2.5 people per household gives 1,000,000 / 2.5 = 400,000 households. If about 1 in 20 households owns a piano (low 1 in 50, high 1 in 10), that is 400,000 / 20 = 20,000 pianos. Units: people ÷ (people per household) × (pianos per household) = pianos.

steps.prompt: How many tunings per year does that imply?
steps.html: About one tuning per piano per year → 20,000 tunings. Many home pianos are tuned less often and concert pianos far more often, so treat one per year as a middle value, not a fact.

A tuning takes about two hours including travel, so one tuner does about 4 per day. Working about 250 days a year gives 1,000 tunings per tuner → 20,000 / 1,000 ≈ 20 tuners. Units: tunings per year ÷ (tunings per tuner per year) = tuners.

steps.prompt: Which bound would you test first to see whether the colleague could still be right?
steps.html: Push every factor to the high end: 1 in 10 households, two tunings a year and 2 tunings per tuner per day (500 a year). That gives 40,000 pianos × 2 / 500 = 160 tuners. Even under these generous assumptions the answer is far below 2,000, so the claim needs a reason this sketch leaves out, such as a region much larger than the city.

blocks.result: About 20 tuners, so 2,000 is off by a factor of 100. The claim needs a very different assumption to survive.

blocks.instructions: Change each factor and watch which one moves the answer most across its plausible range.
blocks.debrief: Factors with the widest relative range dominate the uncertainty. Spend your research effort there.

chart.ariaLabel: Estimated piano tuners as the share of households with a piano changes

interpret.html: Over 200 tuners needs a very high piano share or very slow tuners. Check your assumptions.

assumptions: One tuning per piano per year

blocks.task: Estimate how many litres of coffee an office of 200 people drinks per week.
hints: Factors: people × share who drink coffee × cups per day × volume per cup × days.
blocks.solution: 200 × 0.6 × 2 cups × 0.2 L × 5 days ≈ 240 L per week.

blocks.task: Estimate the number of words you will read this year, with no hints. Name the factor you are least sure about.
blocks.solution: One answer: 250 words per minute × 60 minutes per day × 365 days ≈ 5 × 10^6 words. Reading time per day dominates the uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Which decomposition can you actually estimate for “litres of fuel sold in a country per day”?
options: Cars × kilometres per car per day × litres per km

feedback.1: GDP and price do not combine into a volume without more assumptions.
feedback.2: 42 is not an estimable factor; you would need litres per station.

questions.explanation: Each factor is a quantity you can reason about, and the units cancel to litres per day.

questions.prompt: Your bounds for a factor are 10 and 1,000. What point estimate does the geometric mean give?
questions.feedbackWrong: 505 is the arithmetic mean: it ignores that the bounds differ by a factor of 100. Multiply the bounds, then take the square root.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words why multiplying several rough guesses can still give a usable answer.
rubric: Mentions when they do not (shared bias)
questions.model: If errors are independent, some guesses are too high and others too low, so the product drifts less than each factor's error suggests. Shared bias breaks this.

blocks.task: A news story says a festival “used 3 million plastic cups”. Attendance was 80,000 over three days. Is the figure plausible? Show your factors.
rubric: Compares the estimate with the claim within a factor of 10
blocks.model: 80,000 × 3 days × ~5 drinks ≈ 1.2 million cups. 3 million is within a factor of 3, so it is plausible if cups were not reused; drinks per person dominate the uncertainty.
